European Council President António Costa proposes cutting the EU's 2028-2034 budget by nearly €200bn, a 10% reduction, to win over frugal countries. Cohesion funding is cut for the first time. A 3% digital services levy replaces a controversial corporate tax, and debt repayment is slowed down.

European Council President António Costa has presented a new EU budgetary proposal in a bid to win unanimous support by the end of the year. Still, it is already facing significant opposition ahead of a key European Council meeting on Thursday.

Costa took over the sensitive negotiations on the 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) after the Irish presidency of the Council proposed significant cuts in October.

Ireland's plan failed to win over the so-called frugal countries, including Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden, a powerful bloc of net contributors pushing for a smaller overall budget.

To meet their demands, Costa cut a further €49bn in current prices. The budget would shrink from nearly €2 trillion in the Commission's proposal to €1.78 trillion, a 10% reduction worth €204bn.

Costa's move is an attempt to satisfy the frugals' demand to cut the budget by "several hundred billion euros" and to secure support from all the member states before the end of the year.

"I am confident that this proposal is a good basis for moving towards a final agreement for three reasons. First, this is a budget that matches our ambitions. Second, it keeps national contributions within reasonable limits. And third, it includes a balanced basket of new own resources," Costa said, presenting his proposal.

However, the cut is more modest in 2025 prices, and the proposal includes postponing the repayment of EU joint debt, which the frugals are unlikely to consider a reduction.

An eventual delay in the agreement on the budget would mean several EU programmes would not be ready in time for 2028, and the negotiations would be further complicated by elections in several key countries like France, Italy and Poland.

"The new negotiating framework for the next multiannual European budget is very disappointing," a source from the Élysée told reporters. "As it stands, this proposal from the President of the European Council does not constitute a basis for an agreement."

Meanwhile, the budgetary negotiations have already been made more complex as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said there will be no agreement without unanimous financial support to Ukraine, prompting a backlash from several member states.

Costa's proposal will be the basis for the discussion of EU leaders at the special European Council starting on Thursday in Brussels.

Spending programmes

The fight is not only over the budget's size but over where the money goes. The frugals prefer to be called "modernisers" and want more spending on emerging priorities such as competitiveness and defence.

On the other side, 17 countries from southern and eastern Europe form the "Friends of Cohesion" group, which wants to protect funding for low-income regions through cohesion policy.

Given the group's size, cohesion had barely been touched in earlier compromise proposals. Costa breaks with that for the first time, proposing a €54bn cut for agricultural, fisheries and cohesion funding, around 5% less than the Commission's proposal.

Competitiveness and defence take deeper cuts: €95.5bn, or 16% of the original proposal. Global Europe is hardest hit, losing €45bn, or 21% compared with the Commission's plan.

Administrative costs fare slightly better than under the Irish plan, with a nearly 8% cut to €108bn in current prices rather than 9%.

The Commission's original proposal was already higher than the current budget, so despite the cuts most funding programmes would still see an increase compared with the ongoing MFF.

New digital levy

A key element of Costa's proposal is an ambitious mix of new or revamped EU-wide taxes meant to fill the bloc's coffers with €64bn a year in current prices.

The main novelty is a digital services tax of 3% on annual net turnover from online advertising, digital intermediation services and monetisation of user data. It would apply to companies with EU turnover above €50 million and global turnover above €750 million.

The European Parliament originally proposed the levy, which already exists in France, Spain and Italy. Costa introduced it to replace the Corporate Resource for Europe (CORE), which met insurmountable opposition from member states because it ran counter to the EU's competitiveness agenda.

Opposition to the digital levy mostly stems from fears of US trade retaliation, as most tech giants of that size are American. The calculus appears to be that a Trump administration weakened by its midterm defeat will be less inclined to retaliate.

"These measures would also help create a level playing field in the single market, where American digital giants often face lower taxes than European firms," MEP Danuše Nerudová (Czechia/EPP) told Euronews.

Parliament estimated the levy could raise up to €25bn a year with a 5% call rate and a wider range of online services. Costa's version stays closer to the Commission's estimate of €5bn a year.

Other EU taxes

With CORE abandoned, the most controversial new own resource is the proposal to channel 30% of Emissions Trading System (ETS) revenues to the EU budget, which still faces strong opposition, most notably from Poland.

The Irish presidency had already proposed phasing it in for member states via the Modernisation Fund. Costa goes further with a gradual start: 0% in 2028, rising to the full rate in 2034.

Costa also keeps the proposal for a minimum tax rate of 15% on tobacco and related products. To address opposition from the most affected countries, it would be phased in, starting at 5%, rising to 10% after three years and reaching 15% in 2034.

The compromise also raises the call rate on non-recycled plastic packaging waste from €0.80 to €1.25 per kilogram in 2028.

A less controversial levy concerns member states' contributions based on the amount of uncollected electronic waste. The compromise raises it from €2 to €2.25 per kilogram.

Arguably the least controversial new resource is the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a tariff on carbon-intensive imports. Costa proposes raising the share of revenues going to the EU budget from 75% in the Commission's proposal to 100%.

The proposal also gives a mandate to explore a new levy on crypto-assets, another Parliament idea. The tax was deemed not ready to generate revenue from 2028 and needs more technical and legal work.

A proposal from Eurogroup President Kyriakos Pierrakakis, who is also Greece's finance minister, to feed the EU budget with revenues from the allocation of radio spectrum for 5G and 6G networks has also been picked up for specific radio bands.

Joint EU debt

Costa's plan also cuts repayments of NextGenerationEU debt for 2028-2034 by €10bn in current prices. That is a significant reduction given the recent spike in interest rates, which has pushed up repayment costs.

Repayment of the post-pandemic joint debt would still run from 2028 to 2058, but its "profile" has changed, an EU official told reporters, without detailing what that means for rolling over existing debt with new debt.

"We slightly change the way the capital is paid," the EU official said. "It will start being paid as of 2028. Not in the same amount, but it will start being paid as of 2028."

During cleaning and excavation works carried out at the site, significant remains were uncovered and carefully documented by archaeologists.

The architectural complex around and beneath Hagia Sophia never ceases to amaze.

Six underground spaces, nine tunnels and almost 3,000 tonnes of soil are revealing unknown facets of the monument's history.

An underground world, unknown until now, is gradually being uncovered beneath Hagia Sophia. Galleries, ancient water networks and architectural remains, which may date back to a period earlier than the construction of the present-day basilica in the 6th century, are coming to light during restoration work on the historic monument. So far, 420 metres of underground tunnels have been cleaned, while the Turkish authorities are considering opening some of them to visitors, offering a new perspective on the history of Byzantine Constantinople.

The scale and importance of the work was presented by the Turkish Minister of Culture and Tourism, Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, who went down into Hagia Sophia's underground installations, accompanied by scientists involved in the restoration programme. The Turkish television network CNN Türk has for the first time shown images of the underground galleries and the work taking place in areas that for centuries remained covered by earth and other materials.

According to the data released by the Turkish minister, almost 3,000 tonnes of backfill materials have been removed from two areas of the monument, the Vizier's Garden and the western garden, while investigations have identified six underground spaces and nine tunnels. The works form part of the extensive programme of maintenance and restoration of Hagia Sophia, which the Turkish authorities describe as the largest of the period of the Republic of Turkey.

Traces of an earlier era

One of the most important finds has been identified in an underground burial structure, known as a rock-cut burial space or underground burial monument (hypogeum), in the area of the Vizier's Garden.

There, cleaning and excavation work has revealed architectural layers at a greater depth than the previously known level of the floor. Scientists are examining whether they belong to a period earlier than the current building of Hagia Sophia.

As Mehmet Nuri Ersoy explained, the works went 1.5 metres below the floor level that was covered with mud, revealing traces of an earlier building phase.

This finding is of particular historical interest, as the present-day church of Hagia Sophia was built under Emperor Justinian, between 532 and 537, on the site of older Christian churches.

For the moment, however, no secure dating of the newly uncovered remains has been announced. The assessment that they predate the current church remains a matter for scientific investigation.

An underground network with nine tunnels

In the western garden of Hagia Sophia, six different underground spaces have been identified, which are connected by nine tunnels.

According to the Turkish minister, three of these spaces were most likely underground parts of the old atrium, the courtyard that was linked to the church complex.

Investigations are continuing in other areas, some of which take the form of elongated corridors, between four and 4.8 metres wide.

Of the nine tunnels, seven have already been cleared of backfill, while in the remaining two work is under way to record and document them.

The total length of the cleaned sections reaches 420 metres.

The longest tunnel is 180 metres long and is of particular archaeological interest, as scientists are examining whether it might be connected with the so-called Roman Road of Constantinople.

This gallery runs parallel to the facade of Hagia Sophia, from the area in front of the Fatih Madrasa towards the visitors' entrance, with a gradient of about 3%.

Its possible link with the historic road network of the Byzantine capital is another field of research, and for now the exact original function of the tunnel has not been confirmed.

The hidden water network of Constantinople

According to scientists' assessments, the underground tunnels of Hagia Sophia formed part of a broader system for managing the waters of historic Constantinople.

Some sections appear to have served in the distribution of water and the removal of rainwater, functions that were essential for the protection and daily use of such a large architectural complex.

Their discovery makes it possible to study more closely the technical infrastructure developed around Hagia Sophia during the different periods of its history.

At the same time, the works are not limited to cleaning the tunnels. They include repairs to the vaults, stabilisation of the masonry and reinforcement of sections that have suffered damage.

In one of the underground spaces, 56 metres long, structural damage has already been repaired along an 18 metre section. Other tunnels are being reinforced with stainless steel elements, to ensure their structural stability.

The underground galleries open to visitors

Beyond the archaeological and historical significance of the works, the Turkish government is now also examining how some of the underground spaces could be used as accessible areas of Hagia Sophia.

Mehmet Nuri Ersoy announced that a special plan is being prepared for presenting the underground structures, with the protection of the monument and the safety of visitors as key conditions.

It has not yet been determined which sections might open to the public, nor has a timetable been announced.

Another issue under consideration by specialists is whether the underground network could be used to improve the ventilation of the monument.

According to the technical assessments presented by the minister, the existing underground opening can currently cover only 3.6% of Hagia Sophia's ventilation needs. Future studies will examine whether some of the historic galleries could contribute to a modern system supplying fresh air, without altering their architectural character.

The history beneath the history

Hagia Sophia, which has dominated the historic core of Constantinople for almost fifteen centuries, continues to be the subject of archaeological and architectural research.

The new investigations are now turning attention to the less familiar parts of the monument, below ground level, where the different building phases and the infrastructure of old Constantinople largely remain out of sight.

In this week’s newsletter, Euronews Political Correspondent Jorge Liboreiro unpacks the fallout from the much-hyped “Yalta 2.0”, describing the outcome as a political nothingburger.

Hype is, by nature, risky. In diplomacy, it can be deadly.

Just ask Donald Trump, who arrived in Shenzhen, China, amid pomp, pageantry and sky-high expectations for a historic trilateral summit with his Chinese and Russian counterparts. But let's look at what actually happened.

The meeting had been dubbed "Yalta 2.0", drawing an intriguing parallel with the 1945 conference that defined the partition of the world in sphere of influence among the victors of the Second World War: the United States, Britain and Soviet Russia.

As it turned out, Yalta it was not. More like a wannabe knock-off. And the leader of the world's largest economy – who appeared to doze off at times during the proceedings – had the least to show for himself as he left China's technology hub.

For Trump, the main – perhaps only – takeaway was the photo opportunity with the other two leaders and the media frenzy it generated. But Trump has long understood politics as a matter of optics, and the picture alone may have been enough.

The joint declaration against nuclear warfare was about as meaningful as a Miss World contestant calling for world peace at a Trump beauty pageant – a format he once owned, so he knows a thing or two about it.

For Vladimir Putin, it was more of a mixed bag.

The Russian president was visibly side-lined at the preceding dinner, relegated to a second-tier table while Trump and Xi Jinping chummily sat together.

His heavy-handed attempt to push Russia's war against Ukraine to the top of the agenda also fell flat. The conflict was conspicuously absent from the ironically titled "Declaration toward Peace", published by the three countries after their 80-minute meeting.

The meeting allowed Putin to cultivate the illusion that Russia – an economy roughly the size of Italy's – somehow deserves to stand on equal footing to the US and China. But that's only a mirage. The truth is Putin's Russia is a country is decline.

For almost five years, Moscow has waged a devastating war against its neighbour, inflicting immense human suffering while failing to achieve its core objectives: toppling the government in Kyiv and occupying the country in full.

When it comes to Xi Jinping, eager to capitalise on America's rupture with its Western allies, the summit was a home run.

As host, the Chinese president set the pace and controlled the stage. He spoke in grand terms, likening nuclear weapons to "a sword of Damocles hanging over humanity" and urging "major powers [to] live in harmony".

More importantly, he used the occasion to reinforce his central message: an alternative to the Western-led world order is possible – and China intends to help mould it.

So, was it really Yalta 2.0? Or just three ageing men sitting around a table? It's a fair question: together, they are 227 years old.

"As far as a new Yalta goes, what was so bad about Yalta?" Putin said at the end of the talks. "Yalta formalised the existing realities, and in today's conflicts, too, we will have to come to terms with the realities on the ground."

Needless to say, Putin had the most to gain from staging a replay of the 1945 Yalta conference, where Stalin's Soviet Union emerged among the victors of World War II. Xi, by contrast, urged leaders to "abandon Cold War thinking" – somewhat paradoxically, given that Yalta helped usher in the Cold War.

For Europeans, however, the timing turned out to be surprisingly convenient.

Just hours after the Shenzhen summit, they gathered in Berlin for a fresh meeting of the Coalition of the Willing. It gave them an opportunity to project unity, demonstrate that they were taking matters into their own hands and, perhaps most importantly, show that they were getting on with business, seemingly unfazed by the noise elsewhere.

Their closing press conference said it all. To put it bluntly, it was a collective shrug.

"A Yalta-style format will not bring peace," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said.

"At Yalta, Europe was divided up. It was parcelled up. And we won't allow anything like that to happen again."

Standing alongside him, French President Emmanuel Macron suggested the Shenzhen meeting lacked the legitimacy to redraw the global order.

"Europeans have taken decisions. They have decided to determine their own fate," he said. "Europe is not a subject on a menu of discussions, but a series of powers who want to build their own future."

Admittedly, there was a tangible sense of relief across European capitals.

For the past two years, Europeans have been on edge, fearing that Trump would lose patience and strike a secret deal with Putin over Ukraine's head.

They have become better at resisting – or building resilience, as we say in Brussels – to that kind of fatalistic thinking. But they remain acutely vulnerable to Trump's penchant for political shockwaves.

The past month has, in fact, been a concerted effort to keep the diplomatic process firmly on track.

European, Ukrainian and US officials have met in Miami, Oslo, Brussels, Abu Dhabi and Berlin, building a close-knit working group to develop security guarantees and recovery plans for Ukraine once the war is over.

It marks quite a turnaround from 2025, when Washington deliberately kept Europe out of the loop and journalists – yours truly included – penned obituaries about Europe's "missing seat" at the negotiating table.

Now, Washington is actively urging Moscow to engage in direct talks with Europe, something Russia has consistently refused to do, despite its seemingly endless fixation with reshaping Europe's security architecture.

Privately, European officials see the US push for multilateral peace talks as evidence that Washington has finally recognised a basic reality: whatever contours a deal has, Europe will have to be involved in both negotiating it and putting it into practice.

And yet, they are under no false hopes. Everybody knows the process is and will remain volatile. Nobody can say what comes next. So far, there is little to suggest that Putin is ready for meaningful negotiations.

In another indication of Moscow's reluctance to engage, Putin invited European leaders to Moscow to discuss their participation in the talks – an offer that hardly inspires confidence. He also declared negotiations with Ukraine over in retaliation for the attack on his prized and heavily defended Crimean Bridge.

And so here we are.

For all the uncertainty, Europeans appear to be increasingly accepting that a resolution to the war may be closer than it once seemed. That means the moment for difficult, potentially painful decisions could be approaching. The question is no longer simply whether Europe will have a seat at the table, but whether it will be ready to make those decisions when the time comes.

Above all, Europeans want to ensure that they – rather than others – get to shape the choices that will determine Ukraine's future.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was also in Berlin, put it unusually candidly, describing the war as a "lose-lose situation" for all parties.

"We are clear about what we will accept and what we won't accept," he said.

"But we are also clear that we stand with Ukraine today, tomorrow, for as long as it takes until this unjust war is over."

Thank you reading Off the Record. We'll be back next week.

A French research team tracked people’s loneliness and dementia risk over 30 years.

People who are almost always lonely may be at higher risk of developing dementia, according to a new study that tracked ageing adults over three decades.

There is no current cure for dementia, which affects 57 million people worldwide. But a combination of genetic and lifestyle factors, such as exercise, alcohol and smoking, can affect people’s risk of developing the condition. According to an expert group convened by the Lancet, social isolation is another risk factor.

Researchers from the University of Bordeaux set out to measure that risk. They found that older adults who were chronically lonely had a 38% higher risk of developing dementia compared to those who never felt lonely.

Notably, occasional loneliness was not significantly linked to dementia risk, according to the study, which was published in the journal Aging & Mental Health.

“This distinction is critical,” said Karine Pérès, one of the study’s authors and a senior researcher at the Bordeaux Population Health Centre.

“While most people experience loneliness at some point in their lives, it is when loneliness becomes chronic and persistent that it may increase the risk of developing dementia,” she said.

The researchers analysed data for 3,777 older adults who were tracked from 1988 to 2018. They classified people as “never lonely,” "occasionally lonely” or “chronically lonely” based on four research visits over an eight-year period. Then they looked at whether the participants developed dementia over the next 20 years.

Roughly one in three people who were never or occasionally lonely went on to develop dementia, compared to about 49% of the chronically lonely group, the study found. Most people in the study did not experience regular loneliness.

Loneliness and social isolation aren’t exactly the same. Loneliness is subjective, and people can experience it even if they live with family or regularly see other people, the Bordeaux team said.

“This vulnerability may also stem from unsatisfying relationships, caregiving burdens, or lack of meaningful activities,” said Yvanna Simon, the study’s lead author.

The study has some limitations. It relied on one question to measure loneliness, rather than a comprehensive assessment, and the researchers may not have accounted for all factors that could influence the relationship between dementia and loneliness. But the findings are in line with previous, bigger studies that found a similar link between dementia and loneliness in midlife and old age.

The Bordeaux researchers recommended that health care workers screen their patients for loneliness and encourage more social activities. More inclusive public spaces that welcome people of all ages could also help, they said.

According to Alzheimer’s Research UK, staying socially engaged in old age can help keep parts of the brain active and reduce changes in the brain that are linked to dementia. But the nonprofit emphasised that no one factor causes dementia on its own.

For example, people who are chronically lonely may also get less exercise and eat a less healthy diet, which may contribute to heart disease and diabetes. Those conditions, in turn, raise the risk of dementia. Social interactions are just another layer.

“Lack of social interactions limits cognitive stimulation, while unresolved social stress leads to an accumulation of biological wear and tear over time,” Pérès said.

An unusually early sudden stratospheric warming event has flipped the polar vortex, leaving analysts worried about rising energy prices.

Europeans brace for what could be a particularly cold winter this year, after an unusually early sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) flipped the polar vortex.

The polar vortex is a ring of westerly winds that keeps freezing polar air locked over the North Pole about 30km above the Earth’s surface.

Sometimes, large atmospheric waves can disrupt this circulation, causing the winds to weaken significantly or even reverse direction. This can cause temperatures in the stratosphere to rise rapidly.

As the cold air from high up in the stratosphere disperses, it can affect the shape of the jet stream as the cold air sinks from the stratosphere into the troposphere, which extends from the ground up to an average altitude of about eight to 15 kilometres.

Europe’s dwindling gas supplies

According to market intelligence provider Montel, forecasters warn that this "heightens the odds of colder temperatures”, more storms, wind and heating demand on the continent over the next month.

However, analysts say this would need to be a “repeated event” to have a sustained effect throughout the winter, as single SSW events are “short-term in nature”.

A severe cold spell could put gas supplies under even more pressure, following warnings from the EU that it may have to curb its gas consumption by seven per cent this winter as stocks hit record lows for this time of year.

Dwindling gas reserves, primarily driven by the war on Iran and subsequent blockade of the Strait of Hormuz – one of the world’s biggest fossil fuel shipping routes – are also set to worsen ahead of a full ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports from January 2027.

The unusually early SSW “might make people a bit nervous”, says Klaas Dozeman, energy forecaster at Brainchild Commodity Intelligence, adding that “most meteorologists remain puzzled on what the effects will be over the coming weeks”.

Can heat pumps save households from spiralling energy bills this winter?

Green technology is cushioning Europe from the ongoing fossil fuel crisis, providing more households with energy security and lower bills.

Solar power, for example, has already saved the EU €44.6 billion in avoided gas imports since the beginning of the US-led war on Iran, which started on 28 February.

But as the days get shorter and darker, it is heat pumps that will offer relief from spiralling energy prices.

Heat pumps, which work by capturing energy from air, water or the ground and turning it into heat or cold air, typically deliver three to four kWh of heat for every one kilowatt-hour (kWh) of electricity they consume.

Each residential heat pump installed displaces around 1,100 m3 of gas and two tonnes of CO2 per year on average, if the small amount of electricity it uses to run is from renewable sources.

Europe’s heat pumps provide as much heat as the LNG carried by more than 200 tankers, according to an analysis from the European Heat Pump Association published in June*.

This is double the amount that arrived in the EU in 2025 from the Middle East and around seven per cent of the EU’s total annual imported LNG – avoiding €9.7 billion in import costs last year.

“Every heat pump installed is another bolt in the door of European energy security,” says Paul Kenny, director general of EHPA.

“LNG is the most expensive energy source and comes from unreliable suppliers, and heat pumps can drastically reduce our need for it.”

Despite myths suggesting that heat pumps do not work in cold countries, which Euronews Earth has debunked here, new research has found that when used effectively, air source heat pumps could help heat homes on a typical winter day for as little as £1.84 (approximately €2.20) a day.

Heat pumps more efficient than gas boilers

The study, from British property developers Barratt Redrow, found that heat pumps can be more efficient than traditional gas boilers because they keep a more constant temperature rather than relying on spikes of heat.

"Heat pumps will run during the cold but consume a lot more power,” Jean-Paul Harreman, Director at Montel, tells Euronews Earth.

“The efficiency is better from a heat pump than from a gas boiler, but if power prices go really high, high costs might still be seen during the worst of the cold. However, that is usually only part of the winter, so a price spike should not be confused with an annual total cost.”

Heat pump sales rose 13 per cent last year, hitting 2.9 million in 21 European countries. This brings the total stock to 29.3 million.

When asked whether heat pumps could help the EU’s dwindling gas supply, Harreman said: “A little yes. We see electrification of heating happening in many countries, but the overall impact on demand is not that large.

“Industrial demand destruction plays a bigger role.”

Industrial demand destruction is a sustained or permanent drop in industrial consumption of energy caused by prolonged high prices or supply constraints.

From ski slopes to snow-covered mountain towns, these Asian destinations offer an alternative to Europe’s winter resorts.

When it comes to planning a winter getaway, the chances are you might be thinking of heading to Europe's Alpine destinations in France, Switzerland or Austria.

But if you fancy a mid- to long-haul trip away from the continent, Asia has much to offer with snow-covered mountains, ski slopes and a host of resorts worth exploring.

From the landscapes of South Korea, Vietnam, Lebanon and beyond, these destinations deserve a place on your radar for skiing, snowboarding and other winter adventures.

Karakol Ski Resort, Kyrgyzstan

Kyrgyzstan is definitely worth adding to your winter travel bucket list. Picture fresh powder as far as the eyes can see, amid sweeping views of conifer forests.

On the outskirts of Karakol, a Kyrgyz destination for adventure, the Karakol Ski Resort sits at an altitude of 3,040 metres above sea level in the Tian Shan mountain range, which sprawls across the country, as well as China, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. It is also the highest ski resort in Central Asia.

The season usually runs from late November through to April, with the high season being from 31 December to 10 January. During the winter, daytime temperatures rarely drop below -5C, alongside many sunny days.

Aside from the mild climate, there are an array of residences, from hotel rooms to chalet cottages, within the vicinity.

Mzaar Ski Resort, Lebanon

Self-styled as being “above the ordinary”, the Mzaar Ski Resort is perched above the mountain village of Kfardebian and overlooks the breathtaking Lebanese peak, Mount Sannine.

On offer are 115 kilometres of slopes, 19 lifts and a summit at 2,465 metres, making it the largest ski area in the Middle East. Aside from skiing and snowboarding, the winter season is ideal for ziplining over the mountain or riding aboard a snow groomer.

After a long day outdoors, the resort's wellness area is replete with sauna and cold plunge facilities. While there is an outdoor pool, the indoor one is a year-round option for guests to have a swim and unwind.

Accommodation options include the InterContinental Mzaar Mountain Resort & Spa, which has direct access to the 80km Mzaar Ski Domaine, and L’Escale Du Mzaar, which is just 40m from the first chairlift and has chalets and a ski shop.

O2 Ski Resort, South Korea

This resort in South Korea offers speedy rides 1,420 metres above sea level.

Located in the city of Taebaek, O2 Ski Resort has 16 slopes and six lifts, including one which goes up to the top of Hambaek Mountain, where visitors can take in sweeping views.

Facilities include an extreme park, half pipe and a 136m-long snow sledge, with snow made from Han and Nakdong river sources.

Via the gondola, visitors can head to the resting spot at the highest peak, Eutteum Maru, which overlooks the Baekdu mountain range. Beogeum Maru also offers skiers a place to rest, and is easily accessible to novice visitors as it sits between the beginners' slopes.

Sapa, Vietnam

While Southeast Asia isn’t famed for its snowy landscapes, you should also add Vietnam to your winter must-visit lists.

When the temperature drops over the Hoàng Liên Sơn mountain range – the country's highest peaks – frost and the occasional dusting settle over rice terraces.

In Sapa, the town can transform into a snowy sight from December to late January – occasionally extending into early February. During this time, the air becomes crisp, the mountains become capped by snow and the waterfalls also freeze over.

Vietnam Airlines recommends travellers to add Fansipan Mountain to their Sapa itineraries, which stands at 3,143 metres. The country's highest snow-capped peak is accessible via the Sun World Fansipan Legend cable car.

The carrier also suggests paying Bát Xát Commune a visit, as it receives some of Sapa's heaviest snowfall during the winter. The remote retreat's rice terraces and forests become pearly white landscapes during this time.

Meanwhile, Thác Bạc, or the Silver Waterfall, which is on the outskirts of Sapa, is a 200-metre cascade that frequently freezes.

Shahdag Mountain Resort, Azerbaijan

On the outskirts of Gusar city in Azerbaijan’s Greater Caucasus mountain range, the Shahdag Mountain Resort takes its name from Mount Shahdag, which stands 4,243 metres above sea level. This ski and snowboarding playground features 45 kilometres of pristine terrain, including a selection of 37 slopes and a network of 20 lifts.

Winter paintballing, mountain trekking, snow tubing as well as horseback riding are some of the other activities on offer at the resort during the winter. Visitors are also spoiled for choice when it comes to dining with more than 20 venues among five hotels.

At the backdrop of all this are pristine glaciers, deep ravines, stunning canyons and a variety of flora, fauna and wildlife.

Shymbulak Mountain Resort, Kazakhstan

The Shymbulak Mountain Resort is located in the gorge of Trans-Ili Alatau, within the city limits of Kazakhstan's cultural hub, Almaty. The resort itself sits at an elevation ranging from 2,200 metres to 3,180 metres above sea level.

With a total of 10 lifts, adventure travellers are treated to slopes with a total length of up to 20 kilometres and elevation difference of up to 920 metres for both beginners and experts.

The resort features a range of accommodation options, including the Nero Bianca high mountain chalets, which features its own sauna.

Meanwhile, the Le Mont boutique hotel welcomes guests, including those with four-legged companions. It has a viewing platform, with the panorama of Almaty and snow-capped peaks on display. Other options include Shymbulak Resort Hotel and Tenir Eco Hotels.

Zao Onsen Ski Resort, Japan

The Zao Onsen Ski Resort in Yamagata sits amid mountains and vast wilderness, offering a winter playground where the longest run is more than 10 kilometres long.

The Japanese resort features 32 lifts, ropeways and a gondola that goes up to the 1,661-metre summit station. Experienced skiers can enjoy ski jumps, while there are also routes that run through forests for skiers and snowboarders alike.

At the top lifts, keep an eye out for what the locals call "Juhyo", or snow monsters, that the area is known for during the peak of winter in February.

A combination of Siberian winds and heavy snowfall turn the Alpine trees into giant, monster-like figures. There's even a Zao Snow Monster festival where snow monster mascots entertain visitors.

Soil degradation could cost the EU between €286 billion and €509 billion over its next long-term budget if losses stay at current levels, campaign group Save Soil estimates, urging the bloc to pay farmers for measurable gains in soil health through its next farm subsidy scheme.

Damaged soils could drain €286 billion to €509 billion from the EU economy over the bloc's 2028 to 2034 budget if yearly losses continue at today's pace, Save Soil estimated on Thursday.

The global campaign group wants the next Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the EU's farm subsidy system, to reward farmers for proven gains in soil health instead of leaving them to bear the cost of restoration.

Save Soil was launched in 2022 by Indian spiritual leader Sadhguru and his non-profit Isha Foundation to push governments into adopting policies that protect and restore soils.

Its estimate builds on research by the European Commission's in-house science service, the Joint Research Centre (JRC), which puts the yearly cost of soil degradation in the EU at €40.9 billion to €72.7 billion.

Save Soil multiplied that by the seven years of the next long-term budget currently being discussed in Brussels.

The range covers erosion, contamination, compaction and soil carbon losses, among other damage, and the JRC has noted the bill could double if costs such as biodiversity loss, floods, droughts and health effects were added.

Farm budget talks

In July 2025, the Commission proposed ring-fencing at least €300 billion for farmers' income and crisis support from 2028. On 26 October, EU agriculture ministers agreed their stance on the CAP rules but left funding to the wider budget talks.

Agriculture negotiations at COP31 in Türkiye, ended without a meaningful outcome, with a decision pushed back to 2027.

"Europe is debating hundreds of billions in agricultural support while soil degradation is already imposing enormous costs on its economy," Rico Rau, the lead author of the group's COP31 report, said in a statement.

"The next CAP should not simply compensate farmers for the pressures they face. It should help them rebuild the productive asset their livelihoods depend on," he added.

Risks to the food industry

According to the Commission, 60% to 70% of soils in the EU are unhealthy, weakening their ability to support farming, hold water and cope with extreme weather.

Poorer soils can cut yields, raise costs and make supply chains more fragile, Save Soil warned. The EU's food and drink sector alone turns over €1.5 trillion a year and employs 4.8 million people, according to industry body FoodDrinkEurope.

Save Soil wants the CAP to pay for measurable soil health gains and to reward farmers whose land is already healthy.

It also called for the Soil Monitoring Law, the EU's first soil law, to provide consistent evidence without duplicating measurements and paperwork. The law took effect in December 2025 but sets no binding restoration targets.

Its other two proposals are for the EU's carbon farming certification scheme to reward verified environmental benefits, and for public bodies to use their buying power to secure steady demand for sustainably grown food.

"If we want to ensure food security, farming has to be lucrative," Sadhguru stated in comments shared by the group, adding that governments must make farming profitable or farmers’ children will not take it up.

Five EU countries have agreed to a deal with Rwanda to send rejected asylum seekers there from 2027. The agreement is enabled by the EU's new return regulation, which stipulates that such deals can only be made with countries that respect human rights. Does Rwanda meet that standard?

Five EU countries have unveiled this week a deal to deport rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.

Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece will kick off this plan in 2027, with around 100 single men who cannot be deported directly to their home countries being sent to Rwanda.

The agreement is enabled by the EU return regulation, which entered into force last month. This marks the first time a group of EU member states have used the framework to send irregular migrants to a so-called “return hub.”

Article 14 of this law says that deals to deport migrants can only be made with countries that respect human rights, and many have expressed doubts about whether that is the case for Rwanda.

Freedom House, a US-based organisation which measures freedom around the world, gives the country a score of 7 points out of 40 in political rights and 14 out of 60 in civil liberties. Overall, they label Rwanda as “not free.”

The country also received a score of 0 out of 4 on judicial independence, raising questions about whether migrants not receiving proper treatment in Rwanda would be able to challenge their situation in court freely.

The United Nations Human Rights Council has also said this year that Rwandan authorities “suppress opposition and dissent, prosecuting political opponents, journalists and human rights defenders.”

Meanwhile, Amnesty International notes that Rwanda may be implicated in war crimes because of its support of M23, an armed group in the Democratic Republic of the Congo that is allegedly responsible for summary killings and gang rape. War crimes are amongst the worst possible human rights violations.

The EU Parliament itself has proposed to suspend agreements with Rwanda because of these allegations.

Opponents also point to a precedent: a deal between the UK and Rwanda to send people there while their asylum requests were being processed (so not the same as the EU-Rwanda deal, but similar) was blocked by the UK Supreme Court because it found a real risk that Rwanda would send refugees back to the countries they had fled, which is forbidden by international law.

Rwanda’s government has pushed back and says that human rights are respected in the country and that an independent monitoring mechanism, to which the 5 EU countries have committed, will ensure that.

The parties also say that the UN Refugee Agency will have a role in making sure human rights are protected.
